PHCs in Himachal Pradesh 
*261. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have an y proposal to upgrade the existing 
Primary Health Centres in Himachal Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) the details of funds received fr om the World Bank for upgradation of 
existing PHCs during the last three years; and 
(e) the funds utilised, so far, for the purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (e) Himachal Pradesh has 302 Primary Health Centres (PHCs). 
Recurring and non-recurring expenditure on the PHCs is made by the State 
Government out of their own budget. However, for strengthening the delivery of 
services under the National Health Programmes, assistance is provided by the 
Government of India both in cash and kind. 
*Not recorded.

RAJYA  SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
For providing mother and child health care services, funds are provided 
to States to engage the services of Lab oratory Technicians, additional ANMs, 
staff nurses and equipments. Financial assistance is also provided for 
immunisation and cold chain maintenance activities particularly for conducting 
pulse polio camps, training of functionaries and carrying out of repairs and 
refurbishing of PHCs. Substantial portion of funds released for these activities is 
made out of the World Bank assisted Reproductive and Child Health project which 
is under implementation throughout the country. In addition, an RCH sub-project 
with World Bank assistance is in operation in Kinnaur District since 1997 with an 
outlay of Rs. 3.65 crores. Under this sub-project, 3 Primary Health Centres and 11 
sub-centres are under construction and 39 health care facilities are under repair.

*263. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA:†† 
SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY

(a) whether Government are consid ering reduction in stamp duty on

States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O.RAJAGOPAL): (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Rationalisation of stamp duty all over the country to not more than 
5% by the end of Xth Plan is being taken up as an urban reform measure 
which has been included in the draft Memorandum of Agreement 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati N.P.

(MoA) circulated by Central Government  to the State Governments for which

housing so as to make such units affordable to low income and middle income 
groups as also to increase the housing stock for this category.

so substantial as is being envisaged by the State Governments now. Some 
States have already agreed to sign the Memorandum of Agreement to 
rationalize the stamp duty rates to 5% by the end of Xth plan.This matter is 
being pursued with the remaining States.

SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI : 
Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the schemes and amount allocated for the welfare of 
handicapped persons during the last three years, State-wise; 
(b) the details of the funds utilized, scheme-wise and State-wise; 
(c) the number of handicapped persons benefited under the scheme, State-
wise; 
(d) the number of institutions connected with the schemes; 
(e) whether there is any proposal to increase their number;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (g) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
(a) and (d) A number of schemes and programmes are being 
implemented for manpower development in the field of rehabilitation and for 
providing service to the persons with disabilities through 6 National Institutes, 5 
Composite Rehabilitation centres, 4 Regional Rehabilitation Centres and 82 
District Disability Rehabilitation Centres. The Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment also supports over 800 Non-Governmental Organisations 
(NGOs) under the scheme to Promote Voluntary Action for Persons with 
Disabilities (Umbrella Scheme) and Assistance to Disabled for Purchase/Fitting of 
Aids and Appliances (ADIP). National Handicapped Finance Development Corporation 
(NHFDC) provides soft loan s for self-employment vent ures. Artificial Limbs 
Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO) is manufacturing and distributing 
various types of aids and appliances for persons with disabilities. The National 
Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism , Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation 
and Multiple Disabilities has came into being. Funds under these schemes and 
programmes are not allocated State-wise. 
(b) and (c) Scheme-wise utilization for the last three years and number of 
persons with disabilities benefited under the schemes are given in Statement-I 
{See below). State-wise release of funds for the Scheme to Promote Voluntary 
Action for Persons with Disabilities and Scheme of Assistane to Disabled Persons 
for Purchase/Fitting of Aids and Appliances is given in enclosed Statement-ll and 
III (See below) respectively. 
(e) to (g) Proposals to set up a College of Rehabilitation Sciences and a 
National Institute of Multiple Handicapped have been included in the Tenth Five 
Year Plan. Also the Ministry will continue to expand coverage under the Umbrella 
and ADIP schemes.

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRIMATI

RAJYA  SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
Statement 
(a) to (c) As per the recruitment rule s for the post of Technicians, notified 
on 15th February, 1995, educational and other qualifications required for direct 
recruitment were Matriculation or equivalent and 
(i) A two year trade certificate from an ITI in Radio/TV Electronics/ 
Electrical or equivalent with one year practical experience after 
obtaining the certificate, or 
(ii) A one year trade certificate from an ITI in Air-conditioning and 
refrigeration with two years experience after obtaining the certificate. 
Prasar Bharati has informed that direct recruitment to the post of 
Technician is done by the Head of the Station concerned, who is the 
competent appointing authority in Prasar Bharati. It is possible that some Station 
Heads may have considered cadidates from recognised ITCs as eligible for the 
post. Information in this regard is being collected from about 500 stations. 
Fresh recruitment regulations governing, inter-alia, the post of 
Technician have been notified by Prasar Bharati, on 5th June, 2002, in 
accordance with Prasar Bharati Act, 1990. As per these regulations, the 
educational and other qualifications required for direct recruitment to the post of 
Technician, are Matriculation and at least 2 year diploma in 
Electronics/Telecommunications or equivalent from a recognized institute. 
However, on a call for strike given by the Joint Forum of Akashvani and 
Doordarshan Engineering Employees demanding, inter alia, their association 
in the process of framing of the rule s and regulations, the Prasar Bharati 
Management has, on 18th September, 2002, signed a Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) with them, according to which, there would be 
comprehensive review of these rules and regulations.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
(a) The Judge strength in Supreme C ourt is as per tbe Constitution 
of India. The Judge strengt h in the High Courts is reviewed once in three 
years as per prescribed norms on the basis  of figures of inst itution, disposal 
and pendency of cases in each High Court. As regards District and 
Subordinate Courts, the Judge str ength is worked out by State 
Governments in consultation with the concerned High Courts.

All India Judges' Association & Ors Vs. Un ion of India & Ors, has directed that

lakh people to 50 judges per 10 lakh people should be effected and 
implemented within a period of five years in a phased manner to be 
determined and directed by the Union Ministry of Law. The Central 
Government has filed applications  before the Supreme Court, seeking 
modification of its directions for increase in Judge strength on the basis of 
population in respect of Union territories and permit the Union Government to 
determine the appropriate judge strength based on the relevant factors 
including pendency of cases. The matter is subjudice.

There is no direct competition bet ween the Ayurvedic System of 
Medicine and Allopathic System of Medicine.

of Ayurvedic medicines was affected due to lack of adequate supply of quality 
raw materials, inadequate testing facilities, R&D activities and absence of 
quality assurance. Measures have been taken to address these issues. 
The price of Ayurvedic drugs, raw or finished, is not controlled. 
However, Government have taken steps to augment supply of raw material. 
The Government have also projected t he need for conferring green industry 
and priority industry status to the IS M&H industry in its policy. These 
measures are expected to have positive effect on the cost of production and 
price of Ayurvedic products.

To check the practice of female fo eticide on account of sex selection,

determination and disclosure of sex of the foetus. The Act also prescribes

and fine upto Rs. 50,000.

to ensure a more effective implementation of the Act, amendments have been 
placed on the Table of the Rajy a Sabha on 25.7.2002. Broadly, the 
amendments seek to:

this Act to pre-empt its misuse;

implementation and monitoring of the Act;

(vi) make it mandatory to maintain pr oper records in respect of ultrasound 
machines and other equipments capable of detection of sex of foetus;

for appeals against the decisions of the Appropriate Authority at sub-district 
and district levels, code of conduct for t he persons working in registered clinics

procedures and various IEC activities to create public awareness have been 
undertaken.

(iii)  Pooled Finance Development Scheme (PFDS).

level by Resolution;

Bodies.

transitional costs of moving towards sust ainable and creditworthy institutional

the need for adequate sefeguards for de veloping countries. It is further noted 
that the main safeguards suggested in the Report in  respect of patent regime 
relate to: compulsory licensing; parallel imports; Government use of patent; 
exclusion of diagnostic, therapeutic an d surgical methods from patentability; 
exclusion of new uses of known products  from patentability; Bolar provision; 
prohibition of patent prot ection on plants and animals including genes and 
genetically modified plants and animals; and an obligation to disclose the 
geographical source of the genetic reso urces used in invention in the patent 
applications. The Patents Act, 1970 as amended by the Patents (Amendment) 
Act, 2002 substantially provides for thes e safeguards along with provisions 
which, in sum enable an appropriate timely and efficient response to national 
and public interest requirements/concerns.

developmental schemes and projec ts of North Eastern Region

All the Central Ministries/Departm ents (except those that have been 
specifically exempted) are required to provide at least 10% of their gross 
budgetary support for the North Eastern Region. The unspent balance out of this 
10% is credited to the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR). The 
Department of Development of North Eastern Region provides funds for 
infrastructure development projects from this NLCPR. 
Guidelines have been formulated for administering the NLCPR. 
Procedure for sanction and release of funds from the NLCPR has been 
streamlined. The guidelines have been circulated to all States in the Northeast, 
and can be viewed at the website of th e Department of Development of North 
Eastern Region (DoNER) www.northeast.nic.in During the current financial year 
regular Budgetary Provision has been made in the Demands for Grants of the 
Department of Development of North Eastern Region and Rs. 199.13 crore has 
already been released for 42 projects (40 State projects and 2 Central Sector 
projects). 
The North Eastern Council was set up in 1972, following the enactment 
of the North Eastern Council Act, 1971, to secure balanced development of the 
Region. It prepares 5 Year Plan in consultation with State Governments. In the 
9th Plan against an allocation of Rs. 2114 crores, Rs. 1925.54 crores were 
spent on various developmental Projects/Schemes. For the 10th Plan Rs. 3500 
crores has been approved by the Planning Commission, with an outlay of Rs. 
450 crores for 2002-03. priority areas have been identified in infrastructure, 
human resource development and IT and a focus is being provided to 
completion of ongoing projects and better monitoring. It is planned that with 
these initiatives, the general economic environment in the Region will improve 
substantially. 
The first North East Business Summit was organized on 19-20th July 
2002 in Mumbai in collaboration with FICCI and Indian Chamber of Commerce, 
Kolkata, to showcase the investment op portunities in that region. A one day 
Workshop was organized on 16th February, 2002 in New Delhi wherein 
discussions were held, inter-alia, for augmentation of external assistance in the 
North Eastern States. This Workshop was attended by most of the external aid 
agencies operating in India.

1821. SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: Will the Minister of

corporate; and

lo unleash the productive potential inherent in public sector 
103

enterprises. As per the declared policy of the Government on disinvestment, all non-
strategic PSUs can be disinvested, though the Government may continue the

Price of Medicines 
1828. SHRIAIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the spiraling prices 
of medicines, which have gone beyond the reach of the common-man; 
(b) if so, whether the revised National Health Policy contemplates 
eradication of certain diseases over a de finite period of ti me and for effective 
control of others; 
(c) if so, the details of the programmes, disease-wise; and 
(d) the steps taken to keep the medicines required therefor within the 
reach of the average and poor patients? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) In the changing economy, revision of prices 
of medicines as in other commodities, is a normal feature. While the prices of 
some medicines increase, some others decrease. 
Under the provisions of the Drug (Prices Control) Order, 1995, the prices 
of 74 bulk drugs and the formulations containing any of these drugs are controlled. 
The Government/NPPA fixes/revises their prices from time to time as per formula 
provided under DPCO. In respect of drugs which are not covered under price 
control (non-scheduled formulations), the manufacturers ar e free to fix the 
prices by themselves without seeking approval of Government/NPPA. Such 
prices are normally fixed depending on various factors like the cost of bulk drugs 
used in the formulations, cost of excipients, cost of R&D, cost of 
utilities/packing materials, sales promotion cost, trade margins and quality 
assurance cost etc. 
The Government/NPPA regularly monitors the movement of prices of 
medicines of mass consumption marketed in trade channel and takes action 
whenever instances of unreasonable increase in prices affecting public interest 
adversely are noticed. 
In order to keep a watch on the pr ices of medicines marketed in the 
country, the NPPA regularly analyses the price trends in the market. An 
analyses of date (December, 1998-December-2001) of ORG-MARG, 
115 

RAJYA  SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
which publishes monthly report of "Retail Store Audit Market for 
Pharmaceutical Producers in India" revealed the following position with respect 
of prices of medicines having a minimum annual sale value of Rs. 1.00 crore:

(ii)  The prices of 54%, 51 % and 49% of the above medicines have gone up

treatment of patients suffering from Tuberculosis; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the details of steps taken by Government as a welfare State to 
provide medicines at the residence of TB patients? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) No comprehensive survey in regard to 
prevalence of TB State-wise has been carried out in the recent past. India 
accounts for nearly 1/3rd of global TB  burden. Under the Programme about 1.2 
million TB cases are detected and put on treatment every year. It is estimated that 
almost an equal number of TB cases are detected and treated by non 
jovernmental organizations and private practitioners. 
(b) to (d) Yes, Sir. To control problem of tuberculosis, National TB Control 
Programme has been in operation in the entire country since 1962. The programme 
is integrated with primary health care infrastructure and is implemented through 
a network of 446 district TB centres, 3 30 TB clinics. Under the Programme, all 
diagnostic and treatment facilities, including s upply of anti TB druc^s, are 
provided to the TB patients, free of cost. 
Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), which is an 
application of WHO recommended DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment— Short-
Course) strategy, was launched in 1997 with an objective of achieving a cure rate of 
85% of new sputum positive cases a nd to detect at least 70% of such 
cases.The RNTCP is being implementing in phased manner. The present coverage 
under RNTCP is about 515 million population and it is envisaged to cover 800 
million by 2004 and the entire country by 2005. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA    SABHA 
The project districts have reported a cure rate of more than 80% which means 
that 8 out of every 10 patients di agnosed and put on treatment under the 
revised strategy, are successfully treated, as against less than 4 in the 
previous Programme. 
Under the Programme medicines are given under direct observation by 
a DOT provider. The DOT provider can be a Health Personnel, community 
volunteer or any other individual accessible and acceptable to the patient, 
except for his family members. Theref ore, medicines are not provided at the 
residence of the patient. However, e fforts are made to provide the same 
through DOT Providers at the DOT c entres established as near to the 
residence of the patient as possible.

Review of amendments to the Legal Services Authorities Act 
1900. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that amendments in the Legal 
Services Authorities Act would adversely affect the interest of litigants; 
(b) whether Government agree that  the amendments are intended to 
introduce alternative judicial system and denial of Justice without even appeal 
provisions; 
(c) if not, the opinion of Government thereto; 
(d) the reasons for not prescribing the minimum qualification for non-
judicial members of adalat; 
(e) how far the Lok Adalats comply with Indian Evidence Act; and 
(f) whether Government propose to discuss the matter with Bar Council 
of India and review the amendment? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) to (d) The amendment in the Act permit 
establishment of Permanent Lok Adalats as an additional forum to the litigant 
persons for resolution of their disputes with certain public utility 
188 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
services. Under the Act, it is optional to the litigant persons to approach the 
Permanent Lok Adalats for settlement of their dispute with the public utility 
service. The resolution of disputes through Permanent Lok Adalats not only 
minimizing the litigation expenditure, saves valuable time of the parties and 
their witnesses and also facilitates inexpensive permanent remedy 
appropriately to the satisfaction of both the parties. Therefore, it may not be 
proper to say that the in stitution of Permanent Lok Adalat is anti-litigant.The 
Supreme Court of India has also exam ined the validity of the amendment 
made in the Act in Writ Petition (Civil  No. 543/2002) in the case of S.N. 
Pandey Vs. Union of India, and vide its or der dated 28.10.2002 upheld the 
constitutional validity of the aforesai d Act.The Supreme Court of India has 
also held that the constitution of the Permanent Lok Adalats mechanism 
contemplate the judicial officer or a retired judicial officer being there 
alongwith other persons having adeq uate axperience in the public utility 
services. We do not find any constitutional infirmity in the said legislation. The 
Act ensures that justice will be available to the litigant speedily and impartially. 
We do emphasis that the persons wh o are appointed on the Permanent Lok 
Adalats should be persons of integrity and adequate experience. 
(e) As per Section 22D of the Legal  Services Authorities (Amendment) 
Act, 2002, the Permanent Lok Adalat while conducting conciliation 
proceedings or deciding dispute on merit shall be guided by the principle of 
natural justice, objectivity, fair play, eq uity and other principles of justice, and 
shall not be bound by the code of Civ il Procedure, 1908 and the Indian 
Evidence Act, 1872. 
(f) No, Sir.

Ratio of Judges 
1902. SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN: W ill the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Law Commission had recommended that the ratio of Judges 
per million population should be increased to atleast 50 Judges per million in 
the following five years; 
(b) if so, the ratio of Judges per million at present; 
(c) whether the shortage of Judges is the cause of huge arrears of cases 
in courts; and 
(d) the steps being taken to appoint more Judges so that arrears could 
be cleared? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir.The Eleventh Law Commission in its 
120th Report on "Manpower Planning in Judiciary: A Blue Print" in July 1987, 
inter alia, observed that the strength of Judicial Officers in India was far less as 
compared to certain other countries.The Commission recommended that the 
present strength of 10.5 Judges per million population be increased to 50 
Judges per million population in a phased manner. 
At present, there are 14.7 judges per million population in the country. 
(c) The pendency of cases in courts is, inter-alia, due to various factors 
including shortage of judges, enactment of new laws, increased 
190 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
institution of cases on account of increased awareness of rights on the part of 
the citizens, rise in pupulation, granting of adjournments, industrial development in 
the country, increase in trade and commerce and socioeconomic matters, 
legislative and administrative aspect touching on the life of he citizens of all 
levels, tendency of litigants, lawyers' strike etc. The shortage of judges is one of 
the causes of huge arrears of cases in courts. 
(d) Hon'ble Supreme Court, vide its judgement of 21 st March, 2002 in All 
India Judges'Association & Others Vs. Union of India & Others has directed that 
increase in the judge strength from the existing ratio of 10.5 or 13 per 10 lakh 
people should be effected and implemented within a period of five years. The 
Supreme Court has also directed in the same case that all vacancies in the 
subordinate judiciary must be filled up by 31st March, 2003. 
Central Government have addressed the State Government for taking 
necessary action in increase the judge strength as per the direction of the 
Supreme Court. As regards the directive to be complied with by the Central 
Government in respect of Union Territories, necessary action has been initiated. 
The strength of judges in the Supreme Court is as per the Constitution of India. 
The review of judge strength of High Courts is undertaken once in every three 
years as per the norms prescribed on t he basis of institution, disposal and 
pendency of cases in each High Court.

RAJYA  SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A copy of the Rules is given in the enclosed Statement (See below). 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. A Committee consisting of the Law Secretaries or thier 
representatives from the states of Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Assam was 
formed along with a representative of the Departmet of Justice for framing of model 
Family Courts Rules. Law Secretaries of the Government of Tripura and Sikkim 
also participated in the deliberations. 
The model Family Courts Rules were framed after taking into account the 
Rules of various States and recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee 
on Empowerment of Women in their Fifth Report on functioning of Family Courts. 
These Rules were circulated to all the State Governments and High Courts for 
guidance and for uniformity. 
Statement 
Model Family Court Rules 
In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 23 of the Family Courts 
Act, 1984, the State Government in consultation with the concerned High Court 
may make the following rules:— 
CHAPTER I 
Preliminary 
1. Short title and commencement:— 
(i) The rules may be called the Family Court Rules, 2002. 
(ii) These rules shall come into force on the date of notification. 
(iii) These rules shall apply to the family courts established under Section 
3 of the Family Courts Act, 1984. 
2. Definitions—In these rules,  unless the context otherwise 
requires:— 
(a) "Act" means the Family Courts Act, 1984; 
(b) "Court" means Family Court established under Section 3 of the 
Act under Family Courts Act, 1984; 
192 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) "State Government" means the concerned State Government; 
(d) "High Court" means the concerned High Court; 
(e) "Service" means Higher Judicial Service of the State; 
(f) "Judge" includes Principal Judge/Additional Principal Judge, and 
Judge of Family Court; 
(g) All other words and expressions not defined in these rules shall 
have the same meaning as assigned to them in the Act. 
CHAPTER II 
Terms and conditions of Service of Judge of the Family Court 
3. Service Conditions of Judge, Family Court. 
(1) A Judge of a Family Court shall hold office for a term of five years 
from the date he assumes office or until he attains the age of sixty 
two years whichever is earlier. 
(2) A Judge of the Family Court shall be entitled to the pay and 
allowances including travelling allowance, DA, leave as is 
admissible to a District Judge. In addition he shall also be 
entitled to a special pay of Rs. 800/- per mensem provided that 
pay and allowances of a judge who has retired from the service 
under the Central Govt, or State Govt, shall be regulated in 
accordance with the Central Civil Service (fixation of pay or re-
employed) Pensioners Order, 1986 as amended from time to time 
or in State in accordance with pension rules of the State 
Government. 
(3) The Judge shall be entitled to incur expenditure towards 
contingency to the extent of Rs. 5000/- per annum for 
refreshments served to litigating spouses and their children during 
conciliation proceedings 
CHAPTER III  
Association of Counsellors with Family Courts 
4. Counselling Centre—There will be a centre of counselling attached 
with every Family Court or a group of Family Courts. 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2 002] 
Composition—Counselling Centre may be divided into different units 
and may be located in such other place or places as the High Court 
may direct. 
5. Appointment of Counsellors—Three Counsellors may be attached to every 
Family Court.The Counsellors will be appointed from the panel of 
Counsellors prepared by the Judge of the Family Court and approved 
by the High Court concerned. If it is required, a Principal C ounsellor 
may be appointed out of the Counsellors so appointed who may be 
given a special pay of Rs. 500 p.m. for and above the rates payable 
to a Counsellor. 
6. Qualifications—(1) A person shall not be appointed as a Counsellor unless 
he has attained the age of 35 years. 
(2) A person shall not be appointed as a Counsellor unless he has 
obtained a graduate degree in any of the Social Sciences including 
Sociology, Psychology, Clinical Psychiatry or law and has atleast two 
years experience in the field of social welfare or is associated with field 
work, research or teaching in Govt. Departments or in College, 
University or a similar academic institute in the areas of welfare of 
family or problems of women and children. 
"7. Payment of honorarium/fees to the Counsellors—The Counsellors shall be 
entitled to the payment of honorariu m or fee at the minimum rate of 
Rs. 75/- per sitting for conciliation. In case of reconciled matter, he 
shall be paid Rs- 125/- per sitting. The number of sittings resorted for 
each case should not be more than four. In any case, the total 
honorarium/fees of a Counsellor shall not exceed Rs. 375/- per day. 
8. Panel of Welfare Agencies/medical experts—The Court will also 
maintain a panel of Welfare Agencies or institutions specially in respect 
of matters relating to children in case of guardianship matters and 
may call them as required. They will also maintain a panel of medical 
experts for assisting the court. They will be paid fees @ Rs. 200/- per 
visit or as may be prescribed from time to time by the High Court. 
9. Work by the Counsellors—The Coun sellors may visit (periodically) the 
residences of the parties. They may also be entitled to 
194 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
interview relatives, friends, acquaintances of parties or any of them in 
order to reconcile the dispute. The Counsellor may also visit 
Residence/House of the spouse in a reconciled matter periodically 
and submit his report to the judge. 
CHAPTER IV 
Appearance of legal practitioner or Advocate, Amicus Curiae in 
Family Courts 
10. Appearance of Legal Practitioners or Advocates in the Family 
 Court—Notwithstanding, anything contained in any Law, for the time 
being in force, no party to a suit or proceeding before a family court 
shall be entitled as of right to be represented by a Legal Practitioner or 
Advocate. Provided that if the Family Court considers it necessary in the 
interest of justice, it may seek assistance of a legal Expert as amicus 
curiae. 
Explanation—It does not preclude t he family court from granting 
permission in the exercise of its di scretion, where the circumstances 
justify, to a party to be represented by Legal Practitoner or Advocate. 
11. Appointment of Amicus Curiae—A  Judge will maintain a panel of legal 
experts as Amicus Curiae. At least a panel of five Amicus Curiae will be 
maintained by each Court. Panel of Amicus Curiae will be maintained 
out of the legal experts and also from  the retired judges of local area 
who have expertise in the field. The Amicus Curiae shall be paid a fee 
by the State Governments in a case or proceeding which may be 
determined by the court not exceeding Rs. 500/- per day. 
12. Party entitled to free legal advice—A party will be entitled to take legal 
advice at any stage of the proceedings before the court. A party in 
indigent circumstances will be entitled to free legal aid and advice from 
the State Legal Services Authority in accordance with the rules made 
thereunder by the State. 
13. Panel of Lawyers for free legal advice—The court shall maintain a 
panel of Lawyers willing to render free legal aid and advice. A party 
entitled to free legal aid and advice will be entitled to select 
195 

RAJYA  SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
any of the lawyers from the said panel provided the lawyer is 
available and willing to accept the case. 
14. Circumstances entitling a party to legal aid—The circumstances 
under which such legal aid will be made available to a party shall 
be as determined by the Family Court Judge in each case. 
CHAPTER V 
Procedure in the Family Court 
15. Filing of petitions-Every petition or application shall be 
accompanies by as many clear, authenticated copies thereof as 
there are respondents to be served and by 3 additional copies for 
the use of the court and by such papers as are referred to with 
petition or application. No court fee shall be levied for filing a 
petition. 
(All proceedings instituted before the family court shall be by way of 
petition) 
16. (i) Application of the Provision of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 
(Amended Act of 1976)—The provisions of Civil Procedure Code, as far 
as possible and, as the case may be, shall apply to the proceedings 
before the Family Courts. 
(ii) Save as aforesaid, Chapter IX of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 
(Act No. II & 1974) shall apply in respecty of petitions filed before the 
Family Court.

Development of Cochin Port 
1910. SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: Will the Minister of SHIPPING be 
pleased to state the steps taken during the last three years to develop the 
Cochin Port ? 
202 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
SU.THIRUNAVUKKARASAR): Development of port is an on-going exercise. 
However, the following important projects have been taken up for the 
development of Cochin Port during the last three years:— 
(i) Reconstruction of Boat Train Pier (BTP) Jetty into a multi-purpose Jetty. 
The Port has completed the project of reconstruction of Boat Train Pier 
(BTP) jetty into a multi purpose at an estimated cost of Rs. 17 crores from Port's 
internal resources in the year 2001, which can receive bulk carriers upto 
35,000 DWT. The capacity addition on completion of this project was 0.5 
million metric tonnes per annum 
(ii) Establishment of an International Container Transhipment Terminal (ICTT). 
Tender for this work was invited in 1999. However, due to various 
reasons, it could not be finalised. Fresh tenders have been invited and the process 
of qualifying the bidders is in progress. Capacity addition with this project will 
be to the tune of 5 to 40 million tonnes per annum in phases. 
(iii) Setting up of an International Bunkering Terminal under private 
participation. 
Tender for this porject was invited during 2001 and pre-qualification of 
bidders have been completed. Request for proposals (RFP) have been issued to 
short-listed bidders and due date of submission is 13.12.2002. It is expected that 
capacity addition with this project will be to the tune of 1 million tonnes per 
annum in the initial stage and can go upto 10 million tonnes per annum in the 
final stages. 
(iv) Establishment of an LNG Terminal by the Promoters, M/s. Petronet 
LNGLtd. 
The Port has allotted about 40 acres of its land for establishment of an LNG 
Terminal. The selection of contractors has been completed by M/s. Petronet and 
market tie-up for consumers is in progress. This terminal will handle about 2.5 
million tonnes per annum initially and in the final stages it will handle about 5 
million tonnes per annum of LNG. 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2 002] 
(v) International Ship repair facilities: 
Cochin, with its strategic location, invi ted Expression of Interest (EOI) for 
setting up of a ship repair yard for ocean going vessels to which one request was 
received. This is being examined. This project may take place under BOT format 
or by a Joint Venture approach with Coch in Port Trust. Land for setting up the 
yard will be provided by Cochin Port. Other facilities like berthing, bunkering etc. 
to the vessels will be provided by Port under approved Tariff by the Tariff 
Authority for Major Ports. 
(vi) Special Economic Zone. 
Steps have been taken to develop special Economic Zone (SEZ) to cater 
exclusively for port based industries. Special economic zone is to be located at 
Vallarpadam & Puthuvypeen. State Government has recommended the project 
and Department of Commerce (Govt, of India) has issued in-principle approval on 
27.11.2002. The projects ex pected to be set-up here are Trans-shipment 
Terminal, Bunkering Terminal, Ship Repair Facilities, Port Based Processing 
Industries, Golk Course etc.

Capacity utilisation of Duplo Digital Duplicator 
1926. MAULANA OBAIDULLAH KHAN AZAM: Will the MINISTER OF 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Duplo Digital Duplicat or DP-4030 (4 Nos.) worth Rs. 19 
lakhs are obsolete and Government Press, Ring Road, furnished the capacity 
utilisation of only one machine which is around 7.61 per cent; 
(b) the reason why the data in respect of remaining three machines were 
not furnished to the CAG investigating team; and 
(c) the reasons why his Ministry is keeping mum on this huge loss to 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) 
Four Duplo Digital Duplicators DP-4030 machines were purchased in the year 
1996. The technology of these machines is not obsolete. The Govt. Press, Ring 
Road, did not furnish any "Capacity Utilisation" to the Special Investigation 
Team of Audit. The capacity utilisati on of 7.61% has been assessed by the 
Special Investigation team of the Audit themselves. 
(b) In Govt, of India Presses, Annual Assessed Capacity is fixed 
and capacity utilisation monitored only in respect of main printing machines 
and not for auxiliary machines. Duplo Digital Duplicator machines are 
auxiliary machines used for printing of urgent and short run jobs of 
Parliament and Gazette Notifications etc. Since "Capacity Utilisation" for 
such auxiliary machines is not monitored, data about the same could not 
be provided to the Audit. 
(c) Two out of four Duplo Digital Duplicator machines have already 
given more than 60 lakhs impressions. These have already outlived their 
normal life span and have been used to the maximum extent possible in 
terms of number of impressions also.The remaining two machines are in 
working condition and are being used.There is, therefore, no question of 
any loss to the Govt.

CALLING ATTENTION TO A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE 
Crisis in Plantation Sector and steps taken by Government in this regard 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, with your 
permission, I beg to call the attenti on of the Minister of Commerce and 
Industry to the crisis in the Plantation Sector, namely, tea, coffee, rubber, etc., 
and the steps taken by the Government in this regard. 
THE MINISTER Of DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF 
DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION AND MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE):  Sir,   the Statement 
243   

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
is being circulated to the hon. Members.  Sir, if you want, I will just mention 
some two or three important points from  the Statement. Sir,  the hon. Member 
is completely right in saying that the prices of commodities, which he has 
listed, like tea, rubber, coffee etc., have declined over the last two or three 
years. There are several reasons for this . I have given details of each of these 
commodities, like tea, coffee, rubber, etc. And the main reasons have been, 
firstly, developments in the international market. In the case of coffee, because 
of changes in the value of Brazilia n and Zimbabwe currencies, - their 
currencies have been devalued by almost  50-60 per cent -- there has been a 
significant impact on coffee prices. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK) in the Chair] 
In the case of tea also, the prices have fallen by almost 26 per cent in 
2000-2001. As far as coffee is conc erned, at the moment, the Robusta price is 
80 per cent below the peak level of 1995; similarly, for Arabica also , the prices 
have fallen. In the case of rubber, the h opeful feature is that  the situation has 
started improving considerably.. 
उपसभाध्यक्ष (Ǜी रमा शंकर कौिशक) : मंतर्ी जी, आपको यह ÎटेटमȂट पूरी पढ़नी है।

Sir, in recent years, the prices of commodities in the international 
markets are, generally, depressed, an d this has had its effect upon the 
commodities produced and exported by  India. The domestic price of 
commodities like coffee, tea, and natural rubber have a tendency to move 
244 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
more or less in tandem with the inter national prices. One oT the factors that 
has caused this fall in the internati onal prices is that demand has not kept 
pace with the supply of these commodities. 
The prices of tea, co ffee and natural rubber have declined over the 
past few years. The international price of  tea, after reaching a peak in 1997, 
registered a steady decline from 1999 onwards. There was a 26 per cent 
decline in the international price of tea In 2001, as compared to the peak level 
price of 189 cents per kg. in 1997. T hough the domestic price of tea increased 
from Rs.67/- per kg in 1997 to Rs.76/- per kg in 1998, there has also been a 
steady decline in domestic prices of t ea since 1999 onwards. The decline in 
international prices, coupled with problems like decreasing exports and low 
rate of growth in domestic demand, ad versely affected the domestic prices of 
tea, which declined from Rs.72.79 per kg in 1999 to Rs.61.66 per kg in 2001. 
The average price for the first quarter of 2002 is Rs.47.62/- per kg. 
Similarly, in the case of coffee, prices have been affected the most 
since 2000. The situation over the last  two years remains unfavourable to the 
coffee growers, in India, as well as in  major producing countries like Brazil, 
Columbia, Indonesia and countries in Africa. International prices of two 
coffees, namely, Arabica and Robusta, averaged 130 cents per kg and 53 
cents per kg respectively, in 2001 -- t hese were about 80 per cent below the 
recent peak level price of 261 cents per kg in 1995 ;.n respect of Robusta and 
67 per cent below the peak level price of 359 cents per kg in 1997 for Arabica. 
The domestic prices of Arabica an d Robusta coffee have declined from 
Rs.153/- per kg and Rs.76/- per kg in 19 97 to Rs.72/- per kg and Rs.38/- per 
kg respectively, in October, 2002. 
In the case of natural rubber, althou gh the international situation was 
extremely unfavourable over the preceding four years, the situation has started 
improving considerably from the middle of 2002, with prices recovering in both 
domestic and international markets. While  the present inter national price of 
natural rubber is around Rs.40/- per  kg, the domestic price is around 
Rs.37.50/- per kg - this compares with Rs.28/- per kg during 2001. 
(MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
Domestic and international prices are moving in tandem, and 
because of this development there is some relief amongst the growers of 
natural rubber. 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
The continuous fall in prices of  tea and coffee, coupled with a high 
cost of production, has adversely affe cted the economy of  the plantations, 
resulting in some tea and coffee plantations being abandoned or under lockout 
in the States of Kerala, West Bengal  and Assam. The State Governments are 
primarily responsible for the adminis tration and implem entation of the 
Plantation Labour Act and some State Governments like Kerala, have already 
taken steps to provide relief to the affected plantation workers. The 
Government of India have also taken up this matter with the concerned State 
Governments for intervention and providing necessary relief. 
Sir, the Government of India is fu lly alive to the problems of these 
commodities, and a number of measures have been initiated to deal with the 
current price situation. Some of the steps taken (crop-wise) by the Government 
are : 
In regard to Tea: 
 
 Basic customs duty on import of tea has been increased from 70 per cent 
to 100 per cent from 2002-03 onward. 
Excise duty on tea has been brought down from Rs. 2 per kg. to Rs. 1 per 
kg. in the Budget of 2002-03. 
The Reserve Bank of India had also announced a credit relief package in 
August, 2002, based on the Madhukar Committee Report providing for 
restructuring/rescheduling of the loans outstanding in the tea sector from 
the commercial banks. A review of t he progress of implementation of this 
package has revealed that except for the UBI, implementation has been 
somewhat slow in regard to other commercial banks and the NABARD. In 
view of this, very shortly regional meetings will be held by the Tea Board 
to expedite implementation of this package. 
A factory upgradation scheme has been implemented by the Tea Board to 
encourage production of good quality, orthodox and" non-reconditioned 
CTC teas in the country. 
Government has also provided financial incentives to the exporters of tea 
for meeting part of cost of handling, packaging, transport/freight charges. 
246 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
A Quality Upgradation Programme is being implemented by the Tea 
Board for improving quality of tea m anufactured by small growers in the 
country. 
Due to sustained efforts under t he Quality Upgradation Programme and 
the financial incentives given under  the new Factory Upgradation Scheme 
of the Tea Board, several tea factor ies in the small sector have started 
producing good quality teas with the help of fine leaf procured from 
growers, who have started adopting the recommended cultural practices. 
Such teas have been fetching better prices of late, and this has also 
enabled small growers to realise better leaf prices. 
In addition to the above measures, specific to the question of closed 
tea gardens, the Central Government unde r Section 16(B) of the Tea Act of 
1953, proposes to appoint Expert Commi ttees to make an in-depth study of 
these gardens in each State, and to suggest a package of measures for their 
viability and revival. This concerns, Sir, those estates which have been closed 
or are under lock-out. 
Sir, on coffee, similar set of measures has been taken. 
Coffee: 
Term and crop loans of coffee growers have been restructured under 
a new relief package by consolidating these loans into a Special 
Coffee Term Loan (SCTL) with repayment period of 9-11  years, and 
repayment holiday of three years.  The package includes grant of 
fresh loans, reduction of interest rate on SCTL by one per cent, 
deferment of interest due on SCTL  during the current year to be 
recovered over the next three years, and so on. 
A review of the progress of the Special Coffee Term Loan (SCTL) 
Restructuring was undertaken by the Department of Commerce on 
the 5 m of December, 2002 with the Reserve Bank of India, 
commercial banks and the NABARD. The total eligible account-
holders for SCTL for all commercial banks were 24,297 involving an

SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, for giving me this opportunity to participate in the observation 
of this Bill. I support this Bill. This is a very simple Bill, but yet very significant. 
Sir, India has about 3.3 lakh square ki lometres of land, and it has a vast 
coastline of about 8041 kilometres. Very few countries are blessed with such a 
vast coastline. According to the UN Re solution, the Law of Seas, adopted in 
1982, the coastal States hav e specific rights and jurisdiction for exploiting and 
exploring the mineral wealth. By virtue of that, we have got another eight lakh 
square kilometres, with the result, we have about 33 lakhs square kilometres 
of sea area for mineral exploitation. This is almost as much as the land area. 
During these years, we have not been properly exploiting, thereby we have 
deprived ourselves of very precious mineral wealth. As I said, this Resolution 
was passed in 1982, and, as the hon. Minister was saying, a Working Group 
was constituted in the year 1993; sometime later, in 1996, we accepted this, 
and then, in 2002, we are coming out with the legislation. I feel, Sir, that such 
an important legislation should have been brought before Parliament much 
earlier. Sir, while supporting this Bill, I have few suggestions to make. One is: 
the intent and purpose of this Bill is to regulate and develop. It is not only 
development, but also regulation. Now, we  have a vast coastline, and a large 
number of minerals are available in the sea. It would be very difficult for the 
Government to regulate it. It has got so many responsibilities. Therefore, a 
regulatory body should be in place. It should be a regulatory body consisting of 
professional people. There should not be any Governmental interference. A 
regulatory body is very essential for properly regulating the offshore 
exploration activities.   This is my first suggestion. 
There is a provision in this Bill for collecting royalty on the minerals. 
The rates of royalty on different minerals are different. There is also a 
provision for collecting fixed rent by the Government. As the hon. Member, 
Shri Prithviraj Chavan, said, the State Governments should also have a role in 
this. They are providing the infrastructure; they are providing various other 
facilities. Therefore, my suggestion is t hat, at least, 50 per cent of the royalty 
that is collected by the Central Gove rnment should be given to the State 
Governments. For eleven years, from 1986 to 1997, if my figures are correct, 
the Central Government had collected Rs.643 crores. It is a very meagre sum, 
compared to the potential. With the passage  of this Bill, this amount could be 
increased and the Central Government should share this money with the State 
Governments.

THE WILDLIFE (PROTECTION) AMENDMENT BILL, 2002 
THE VICE CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA): Now, we will 
take up the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Bill, 2002. 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMEN T AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Wild life (Protection) Act, 1972, be 
taken into consideration." 
Sir, as this august House is aware, the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, 
provides for protection of wild animals , birds and plants, management of their 
habitats, and regulation and control of  trade in the products derived from 
various species of wild animals. This legislation, made three decades ago, is 
the testimony to our will and vision for protecting the environment and ecology. 
Wildlife is the barometer of the health of the forests and holds the key 
for India's water resources and also for food security. More than 600 million 
people depend for their livelihood on forests, wetlands, grasslands and coastal 
areas. India's National parks and Sanct uaries are the cradles of our rivers, 
lakes and water resources, with nearly 300 rivers originating from there. 
Despite having only 2 per cent of the ge ographical area of the world, India 
takes pride in possessing 50 per cent of the global Tigers and Asiatic 
elephants, and 65 per cent of the one-homed Rhinos. Besides, the only 
surviving population of Asiatic lions are fo und in this country. In India, forests 
and protected areas play a crucial role in harbouring 8000 known medicinal 
plants in the wild. The demand for medicinal plants is growing, and a large 
proportion of India's population prefer s naturopathy to allopathic medicines. 
This august House is aware that the quality of environment is intricately linked 
with the nature and the unique biological resources that have been bestowed 
by Mother nature. Bio-diversity conservation cannot be restricted to national 
parks and sanctuaries alone. Areas which are outside the network of protected 
area form vital ecological corridor to protect wildlife and maintain its continuity. 
In 1970, there were only 65 protec ted areas, we have now been able 
to establish 587 national parks and wildlife sanctuaries in the country. 
305 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
The population of important species like ti gers, elephants, rhino, lion etc. has 
improved satisfactorily because of the sustained efforts made by the Centre as 
well as the States. However, a need has  been felt for further strengthening the 
provisions pertaining to several important aspects. 
During January this year, the hon.  Prime Minister had released the 
National Wild Life Action Plan highlighting the policy and the actions to be 
adopted for the conservation of wildlife. The Wild Life conservation Strategy, 
launched by the Hon'ble Prime Minister, recognizes the fact that while wild life 
is important, protecting the interests of  the poor and tribals, living in and 
around the protected areas, is also equally important. This can be achieved by 
maintaining cordial relationship between the people and the managers. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, with this backdrop, I now bring the important 
features of the proposed amendments to the attention of the hon. Members. 
An important provision made in this Bill seeks for creation of two new 
categories of pr otected areas, i.e., "Conservation Reserve" and "Community 
Reserve". These reserves would preferably link the national parks and 
sanctuaries for the protection of wildlife  and its habitat. However, they will be 
managed by the local community in a transparent and participatory manner 
involving the members of village Panc hayats, NGOs, and other experts. The 
declaration of these two reserves ai ms at improving the socio-economic 
conditions of the people living in those areas as well as conservation of wildlife 
through sustainable utilization of forest produce. In addition, it is also proposed 
that the existing wildlife sanctuarie s are managed in a participatory way with 
the involvement of representatives of Panchayati Raj Institutions, NGOs and 
other experts. 
The existing provisions do not prescribe any time limit to settle the 
claims of the people after the notification of  intent is issued in respect of 
national parks and sanctuaries. As a resul t, the objective of conservation has 
got a setback and several sanctuaries and national parks have been put to 
misuse and encroachments. It is now proposed to limit the period of settling 
the claims to two years. 
At present, the Indian Board for Wild Life (IBWL), under the 
Chairmanship of hon. Prime Minister, is the highest advisory body at the 
National level "for promoting conservation and controlling poaching through 
306 

[9 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
coordinated policy and administrative measures. The Bill seeks that the 
National Board is given statutory status  and is renamed as the National Board 
for Wild Life. Similarly, the State level Boards, headed by the Chief Minister of 
the respective State, are to be renamed as the State Board for Wild Life. 
At the time of enactment of the 1972 Act, many persons who had in 
their possession wild animals and their derivatives belonging to Schedule I and 
Part II of Schedule II could not declare them within the limited period of 30 
days. The proposed amendment will give them one more opportunity. 
Currently, persons having ownership certif icates in respect of Schedule I and 
Part II of Schedule II animals can sell or transfer such articles. This has 
encouraged illegal trade in wildlife products. In order to prevent such activities, 
an amendment is proposed to restrict such transaction except by way of 
inheritance. 
Poaching and illegal trade, if not controlled effectively, have the 
potential to nullify all achievements made so far in wildlife conservation. 
Stringent provisions are, t herefore, proposed for forfei ture of the properties of 
criminals who have been convicted in the past for heinous wildlife crimes. 
These provisions are similar to the pr ovisions of the Narcotic Drugs and 
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. 
Presently, the penalties for committing offences lack in severity. It is, 
therefore, proposed that th ese are enhanced from a minimum of one year to 
three years extendable to seven year s besides doubling the fine from the 
existing Rs.5,ooo/- to Rs.10,000/-. In  order to improve the intelligence 
gathering in wildlife crimes, the existing provisions for rewarding the informers 
are sought to be amended so as to enhance the reward from 20 per cent to 50 
per cent, and a reward of up to Rs.10,000/ - is also proposed to be given to the 
informant by the State Government. 
Unregulated growth of zoos in the country has seriously affected the 
quality of zoo management. It is, theref ore, proposed that no new zoo shall be 
established without prior ap proval of the. Central Zoo Authority. Sale and 
transfer of scheduled animals by zoos will also be regulated to prevent illegal 
transaction. 
307 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2002] 
Encroachment in the sanctuaries and national parks is a matter of 
serious concern for bio-diversity conserva tion and integrity of the area. Hence, 
the proposal has been made to empower the officials to evict such 
encroachments. Besides, . some ot her changes of consequential and 
incidental nature have also been proposed in the Bill. 
I hope this Bill, which seeks to further the cause of protection of 
wildlife of the country, is a non-controversial measure,  and, hence, will find 
support of the House. 
With these words, Sir, I beg to move for leave for consideration of 
Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Bill, 2002. Thank you, Sir. 
The question was proposed

adopting the following approach: 
The main objective of disinvestment is to put national resources and 
assets to optimal use and, in particular, to unleash the productive potential 
inherent in our public sectc enterprises. The policy of disinvestment 
specifically aims at : 
• Modernisation and upgradation of  public sector enterprises; 
• Creation of new assets; 
• Generation of employment; and 
• Retiring of public debt. 
Government would continue to ensure that disinvestment does not 
result in alienation of national asse ts, which in spite of the process of 
disinvestment, will remain where they are. It will also ensure that disinvestment 
does not result in  private monopolies.
